claims.text: The target material is a quaternary equiatomic, single-phase FCC alloy.
The relevant initial grain size is approximately 1–10 μm.
The target alloy has an SFE greater than 40 mJ/m².
Plastic deformation under uniaxial tension is primarily governed by dislocation glide.
Stacking-fault formation is a primary plastic-deformation process in these alloys.
FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformations occur only at high strain rates or extreme local stresses.
An SFE above 40 mJ/m² suppresses deformation twinning.
An SFE above 40 mJ/m² suppresses deformation-induced phase transformation.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate when SFE exceeds 40 mJ/m².
At low strain rates and high SFE, deformation proceeds by dislocation glide and cross-slip.
Under low-rate, high-SFE conditions, yield strength follows a power-law dependence on strain rate.
High strain rates or low SFE promote FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC deformation-induced transformations.
High strain rates or low SFE can promote deformation-induced amorphization.
Deformation-induced transformations alter yield behavior and strain hardening.
Yield strength increases as temperature decreases from 300 K toward 77 K.
Yield strength increases with increasing strain rate.
Phase transformations are observed only above 10² s⁻¹ or in low-SFE alloys.
High-SFE pure Ni and Cu exhibit strain-rate-insensitive yield strength.
Low-SFE austenitic stainless steels exhibit TWIP and strain-rate-dependent yielding.
The threshold strain rate for transformation depends on local stress concentrations.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says high SFE makes yield strength insensitive to strain rate, while the mechanism states that yield strength has a power-law strain-rate dependence and the predicted outcome says strength increases with strain rate.
The hypothesis allows transformation at extreme local stresses regardless of bulk strain rate, whereas the predicted outcome says transformations occur only above 10² s⁻¹ or in low-SFE alloys.

Transformation below 10² s⁻¹ is declared falsifying, even though the hypothesis and uncertainty fields allow low-rate transformation at extreme local stress concentrations; an in situ TEM specimen could itself contain such concentrated stresses.
